name: Pomegranate Purple
lede: Pomegranate Purple is a deep, muted reddish purple named for the fruit's seeds and rind, dated by the Maerz and Paul dictionary to 1886.

sections.title: The fruit, not quite the color we expect
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates "Pomegranate Purple" to 1886 and plots it on plate 4 I 6 [1]. The name points to the fruit, but the swatch leans more toward a dusty wine red than toward the violet most people picture when they hear "purple" [1]. Its Munsell notation is 2.1R 4.3/9.9, a notation that sits in the red hue band despite the name [1].

The closest of our common colors is [[english-red]], 3.2 units away [1]. The books we hold do not say which part of the fruit, the rind or the juice-stained seeds, the namer had in mind [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, this color appears in only 24, about 0.1 percent, rarer than 66 percent of our named colors [2]. It peaks in the 1600s, in 5 of 6,394 paintings, and inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 92 percent of its matched paintings, rather than a light or a shadow [2].

The earliest match is a 1508 panel by [[painter:juan-de-flandes|Juan de Flandes]], about three and a half centuries before the 1886 name, so that early hit is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of the dye or pigment, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].
